analysis.one_liner: Uses taxpayer money to fund House campaigns in exchange for tight donation limits, party soft-money bans, and mandatory debates.
analysis.headline: A single congressman introduced the bill with no cosponsors in February 1997; it died in the House committee it was sent to, never getting a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a voluntary-feeling system of public financing for House elections. A candidate who collected signatures from 3% of district voters — or whose party won over 25% of the vote there last time — could get federal money (up to $750,000, adjusted for inflation) to run the campaign. In exchange, that candidate could accept no more than $100 from any individual, had to raise 80% of private money from in-state donors, and had to take part in at least two televised debates. The bill also banned national party committees from raising unregulated 'soft money,' required disclosure of big outside election spending, and cracked down on contributions funneled through intermediaries.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates without access to wealthy donor networks — first-time challengers, candidates from modest backgrounds, and voters who would see campaigns funded by small in-state donations and public money instead of large checks. Party committees lose their soft-money channel, and broadcasters face new obligations, but candidates and voters gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: Qualifying House candidates would receive public funds roughly equal to the cost of 2.5 hours of local TV advertising time, capped at $750,000 and indexed to inflation, so they could run competitive campaigns without courting large donors [S2] [S3].

Qualifying candidates could accept no more than $100 from any individual per election cycle, and at least 80% of their private contributions had to come from donors in the candidate's own state, shrinking the role of distant big-money contributors [S2] [S3].

Qualifying candidates would have to appear in at least two televised debates in their district media market, and stations would have to carry publicly funded campaign ads and face audits of the rates they charged [S2] [S3].

The bill banned national party committees, including the congressional campaign committees, from soliciting or spending money outside the act's limits and reporting rules, and required disclosure of election-related spending by outside groups above $2,000 [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who would finance up to $750,000 per qualifying House candidate per election. Broadcasters would be compelled to sell campaign advertising until it made up a set share of their airtime, with their FCC licenses conditioned on compliance. National party committees and large donors would lose a major, lightly regulated fundraising channel.

drawbacks.text: The public cost is real: up to $750,000 in federal money per qualifying candidate, which across hundreds of House races each cycle would run into the hundreds of millions of dollars [S2] [S3].

The bill forces radio and TV stations to accept publicly funded ad orders until campaign advertising reaches 40% of their ad time and ties their license renewal to that obligation — a significant mandate on private broadcasters [S3].

Requiring 3% of a district's registered voters to sign a petition weeks before the general election is a high bar that could screen out minor-party and independent candidates rather than widen the field [S3].
A $100 per-person contribution cap, combined with the public funding level, may leave candidates in expensive media markets underfunded relative to what competitive House races actually cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and clearly laid out: candidates get public money and must rely almost entirely on small, local donations, which would weaken the influence of large contributors and unregulated party money. The honest objections are the taxpayer bill — potentially hundreds of millions per cycle — the compulsory-advertising mandate on broadcasters, and a signature threshold that may be hard for new candidates to clear. It is a serious, detailed attempt at public financing rather than a symbolic gesture, but its cost and mandates would have drawn substantial opposition.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House committee it was referred to for nearly two years, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews (D-NJ) introduced the bill on February 4, 1997, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Oversight [S1] [S5].
No other member of the House cosponsored the bill — the cosponsor count was zero [S4].
The committee took no further action on the bill; the action history shows nothing after the February 1997 referral, and the bill died there when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and the national party committees kept the existing campaign finance system, in which large donations and unregulated party soft money remain legal. Large donors and broadcasters were also spared the new limits and advertising mandates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents and big donors kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.what_they_did: Introduced the public financing bill and was its only sponsor

against.name: House Committee on House Oversight
against.role: The House committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 4, 1997 and never reported it out or scheduled any action on it; the bill died in committee

sides.party_line_note: One Democrat sponsored the bill and not a single member of either party cosigned it, so the record shows one sponsor and no organized support rather than a party fight.

industries.note: The bill would bar national party committees, including the House and Senate campaign arms, from soliciting or spending any money outside the act's limits and reporting rules, and would stop parties from routing funds to 501(c) nonprofit groups. Party committees profit from loosely regulated fundraising, so their interest here runs against voters' interest in limits and disclosure.

Stations would be forced to accept publicly funded ad orders until campaign ads make up 40% of their advertising time, with license renewal conditioned on compliance and random audits of their rates. Broadcasters profit from selling airtime at market rates, and the mandate would override that discretion.

A $100 per-person cap for qualifying candidates, plus the soft-money restrictions on parties, would sharply reduce the leverage of large contributors. Their influence over candidates depends on the current system the bill would replace.

industries.industry: Political advertising and campaign consulting firms
industries.note: Public money could still be spent on ad production, media buys, voter contact tools, and staff salaries, so campaign vendors would remain paid — with the government as a reliable funding source — though at rates subject to audit.
